comments.text:
4:24 – I left the Discord about a month ago after being there for roughly four months.

I think Tim is getting bad information about what's actually happening there, or he's overselling it.

He often says there are "tens of thousands" of people in the Discord. That may be technically true but not reality. During the IRL post-show, which seemed to be the most active event, I never saw more than 300 people online. As for people actually participating, I'd estimate around 75-80, with maybe 15–20 regulars.

If you're expecting to interact with the cast, don't. I never saw any of them participate during the entire time I was there. Employees were also very rare. One of the regular volunteers did get hired, but she was married to an employee. For the most part, the server is run by volunteers.

The volunteers are a mixed bag. Some are genuinely good people who are there to build a community and have conversations. Others seem more interested in acting as unofficial spokespeople, repeating whatever was said on that day's timcast post rather than having an original thought or opinion. Disagree with them, and the conversation can quickly turn into a lecture, even if you're just correcting a misconception. (No names, but my cousin was 101st with one volunteer who hosts stuff...he's greatly exaggerating his service.)

I'll admit I'm disgruntled.

They ran a heavily promoted "Design a Skateboard" contest. I submitted three designs, two original designs I created and one AI assisted design. Two of my submissions made the finals, and the AI design ended up winning.

The prize was supposed to include the skateboard, a shout out, and merchandise. They were supposed to sell the boards too, can't remember if it was discord exclusive or at Boonies HQ. I signed the required paperwork and then waited.

Weeks went by with no communication.

After several weeks, I messaged Mark. No response.

A few weeks later, I followed up again and also contacted the designer I'd been communicating with. Nothing. Total of 9 weeks passed.

I then asked about it in the Discord. My question was ignored while other posts continued to receive responses. 
So I reached out to the only mod that ever actually responded to DMs (and she really was great about handling it as best she could)

She explained that they couldn't legally provide the prizes or sell the board like they originally promised. She was nice, and even offered an autographed skateboard instead.

I appreciated her trying to make it right, but that wasn't really the issue. The problem wasn't the prize, it was the complete lack of communication. Zero ownership of the mistake. And never once an apology. Not to mention the lack of respect. (nod to "Dirty Work")

So I left the Discord and emailed Timcast to explain my experience. I never received a response. So I guess they filter out the complaints or they just ignore them.

I had no intention of talking about this publicly. I even said as much in my email. But every single show Tim mentions the Discord it bugs me that I still never got an apology at the bare minimum. So, I figured people should know what my experience was before they decide to spend their own time or money.

I don't have an online presence, so this will be ignored as well. Whatever, I guess it doesn't even matter.

transcript: A change is coming. It's been bubbling up among the younger generations. Many older people have not been paying attention. And many of us are going to get trapped like Blockbuster got trapped. A downward spiral and eventually business goes tits up. What we're looking at is the AI content revolution. And I don't know how long it will last. It may actually be somewhat shortlived for now, but I do believe that we're looking at a period where AI content is going to take over. And as much as people don't like this, it doesn't matter what you like or don't like. I'm not trying to be mean, but I'll put it like this. I would love to live in a time of Blockbuster video. I grew up in the 90s. I was a kid. And I remember those Friday nights where we'd come, we'd get out of school, go to Blockbuster to rent movies and video games for the weekend, and then you had to return them Sunday night. I'd go to 7-Eleven, I'd pick up, I'd get nachos and candy and drinks, and we'd hang out. Those were the days. And we see these AI generated '90s videos going massively viral because people reminisce and they love it. The truth is technology changed. Blockbuster went by the wayside. And we used to have family pizza huts, play places at McDonald's, but now it's all just brutalist box stores. There strip malls, pizza pickup. They're trying to bring it back because people do miss it. But I believe the AI content revolution is here. And ain't nothing y'all can do about it. Now, for me, uh, I make music. I've written and published several songs along with Carter Banks, who has also, uh, done all the production for all of our music and has helped write, uh, uh, much of it. And we've had some tremendous success. Not like we're major rock stars or anything, but we've had some songs get 30 million or so streams and tens of thousands of sales. In the past few years with AI music content, things have changed dramatically. So, I've noticed a handful of things that we're going to break down in this segment talking about what the future holds for all of you. And the first thing is, well, AI content slop, it's actually getting demonetized. So, there's something that yall need to understand. For those of you that are looking to get into YouTube content creation, podcasting, music, or any kind of art in general, even video games, there's a lot to break down in what we are currently seeing in the changes that are happening and how the machine is actually resisting it. I'll start off by saying this. If YouTube allows this AI content and so does Spotify, there will be no content anymore. Right now, what we are looking at is what's called model collapse, where these AI these AI systems are regurgitating content within themselves and training off of that same content. Eventually, it'll be too difficult to produce original content. The a training models will go insane and then YouTube will cease to function properly as will Spotify. So, what have we seen? Spotify and YouTube are cracking down on AI content. And I can see it in the algorithm. I can see it in the ad rates. Ad rates for content in the space that we occupy, which is news, culture, commentary, politics, etc. has actually gone up a decent amount. And we can see our ad rates, our RPMs, which is money per view we receive, has increased since YouTube began taking down this AI slop content. But despite the fact we could all agree that slop sucks, something else is coming and you need to be prepared for it. So, I'm going to show you a bit of the future. I know whether you like it or not. There are a lot of people I've posted AI generated music and they say this is terrible music. I hate the style. I hate the genre. And you're allowed to. That was always allowed. The point is not that the genre, the style, the songs are good, but that I can snap my fingers and produce a top tier Hollywood level song 15 minutes. The changes now. We'll start here with YouTube and then we'll get into the music, Spotify, and what's happening. important things that you all need to understand, but but also does stretch into governance with flot cameras and things of that nature. So, before we get started, my friends, make sure you head over to timcast.com to join our Discord community. We got tens of thousands of people hanging out every single day, and you got to be the change you want to see in the world. The conversation around AI is big, and it's not all bad, but it is bad in a lot of ways, and it's a way in ways that we should have a a conversation about. Join us at timcast.com to support the work that we do. Smash the like button. Share this video with everyone you know. Don't forget to subscribe. Let's start here with Hollywood Reporter from June 13th. Faceless creators take a hit as YouTube cracks down on AI slop. Just a few years ago, they were raking in clicks and cash, but now that the platform tweaked their algorithm, they're suddenly collateral damage. I saw this right away. A year or so ago, we began to experience what I would describe as an in industrylevel problem. Particularly for those of us that work in podcasting as well as we call this vodcasting, video podcasting. It's weird neologism as it were. Ad rates were going down, viewership was going down. And we knew exactly why. In fact, I've talked about it quite a bit. Young people, early 20s, had figured out how to mass generate YouTube content. Now, this these videos don't get a lot of views. Sometimes they'll be a banger, but for the most part, they might get 800 views. Now, you may be thinking, what's 800 views? Well, honestly, it's nothing. If we just round up, let's just do simple math and say a,000 views. These people might be generating somewhere between five and $10 per video. And this is where it gets bad. They were producing hundreds of videos per week. So, actually quite simple. If you make a hundred videos and you're averaging between five and 10, you might actually within a matter of two days pull in, I don't know, 500 to $1,000, if not more. And well, I I yeah, somewhere around there. By the end of the week, if you've produced somewhere close to 500 to a,000 videos, you could be looking at six figure income. Some of these guys that went viral gave interviews where they were generating between 100 and $200,000 per month autogenerating long form and short form content, but it was killing the platform. People aren't returning to watch these videos and so long as the algorithm promotes them, you're getting content that is not meaningful and doesn't attract an audience to stay on the platform. So, this is a problem for YouTube and much to my surprise, YouTube began to demonetize these channels. Surprise, surprise. Many of these channels, not all, have stopped producing content outright. What they would do is you would see some of these videos, an example would be stick figures explaining some kind of news event or historical event. There are programs, there are companies where you can pay them and they will autogenerate a video for you. You then get a monetized account. And although you're not going to make a million bucks right away, you pay about $3,000 a week and you make about $5,000 to $6,000 per week by uploading mass amounts of content. But this means that the average person who has only a funded amount of time during the day cannot watch everything. And so for us, it's quite simple. The front page of YouTube is a raffle. There's about 15 videos that appear on the front page, sometimes less. Now they've added shorts. It could be a lot less. And this means that if you're producing long- form content, which by far is the most lucrative, if if your subscriber, follower, fan goes to the front page of YouTube, and instead of seeing your content, they see one of 1,000 AI generated videos, this just means that while they may not actually prefer that content over yours, because the video appears on their front page, they're going to click it. And this is the game. If they produce a thousand AI slot videos and you produce two or three in a single day, well, the way the lottery works is because there's substantially more of these AI videos, the likelihood that your video surfaces diminishes. The less your fans click on it, the less they recommend it. It's a downward spiral where volume wins against everything. So, YouTube has changed this. They are dealing with this to try and shut it down. And while it has eliminated a lot of these really awful channels, many of them still exist because they've crossed the bare minimum threshold of original content. And that's the world that we are now going to enter. Let me jump next to Spotify. Spotify removes AI slop and seeks transparency from musicians who use AI. In short, Spotify is making it easier for listeners to figure out if the music they are listening to is humanmade or produced using generative AI. While the audio streaming service says it will not get in the way of artists and producers using AI, it's committed to removing AI slop. What's next?
